title: Verstappen assesses Friday performance at the Madring
excerpt:
Max Verstappen admits that Red Bull are still "getting up to speed" ahead of the Spanish Grand Prix, as drivers and teams tackled the Madring for the first time.

Friday provided the first running for teams and drivers at Formula 1's newest venue, with the high-speed street circuit offering a challenge across the day.

Verstappen finished P5 and P6 across the two, one-hour sessions, but was closer to pacesetter Kimi Antonelli in the latter, as the Dutchman finished just four tenths behind.

"Not too bad. Just trying to find a little bit more pace over one lap," said Verstappen when asked on his thoughts from the first day of running.

"Trying to understand the tyres a little bit more in the long run. Just getting up to speed a bit more, lap after lap.

"There's always little things in a practice session you want to work and improve on. That's what we'll try to do for tomorrow and we'll see where we end up."

When asked how important a clean Free Practice 3 session would be on Saturday ahead of Qualifying, Verstappen added: "It will always help if you have a clean one compared to a messy one, but we'll see if we can find a little bit more performance in the car."

Team mate Liam Lawson, still in place for the injured Isack Hadjar, finished both sessions in P10 as Red Bull tried to get on top of the circuit's bumps.

"Is more bumpy than what we thought, high speed corners, Turn 10, 11, 12," said Red Bull's Technical Director, Pierre Wache, who believes the team are still in contention at this early stage.

"It is quite a challenge there for the ride. Energy management is tricky also. I'm not a driver but it's quite challenging.

"Was quite a smooth session. More I would like to be, like a normal Friday. Now we have to improve the car but not completely out is some positive, after we are not completely out [of contention], we know that.

"Some traffic in [the] long run, but the long run was quite competitive to be honest. I think our tyre management, we are quite good."

title: Russell shares ‘big question mark’ facing drivers in Spain
excerpt:
George Russell has shared his concerns around “the big question mark” that will impact the rest of the Spanish Grand Prix weekend, with the Mercedes driver predicting that tyre degradation will play a significant role.

After admitting that his team mate Kimi Antonelli, who leads the standings by 66 points, has done “a better job” this season, Russell went on to top the times in the first hour of practice at the brand-new Madring.

He then dropped to P5 behind the Italian, the Ferrari pair and Racing Bulls’ Arvid Lindblad in FP2, and later offered his thoughts on getting to grips with the latest addition to the calendar.

“It was very fun driving the track for the first time,” he said. “It’s always a great experience driving a new circuit. FP1 was a strong session. FP2 we made some set-up changes – it wasn’t quite as good, so we’ll probably revert back on that. So far, so good.

“I think there’s a big question mark over the tyre degradation. In FP1 with the tyre degradation we all had, we think a six-stop race would probably have been the fastest way!

“I don’t think anybody’s going to do a six-stop race on Sunday and I’m sure tyre deg will be better, but with that big long corner – La Monumental – it really hurts the tyres. That’s going to be a real challenge for everyone.”

La Monumental is arguably the most striking feature of the Madring with its extreme banking and horseshoe shape, but FP1 and FP2 showed that it can be punishing for both the drivers and their tyres.

Mercedes Deputy Team Principal Bradley Lord appeared less concerned about regular tyre degradation, focusing instead on the loss of running that came as a result of Lindblad’s crash on Friday afternoon.

“You could see some unusual tyre effects just because they’re going to be running so hot,” he explained. “You’ve got a lot of cornering sequences without a real chance for the tyres to have a breather around the lap.

“It’s not like it’s corner, long straight, corner – it’s corner after corner after corner. How the tyres cope with that is going to be decisive, so even though it’s a very smooth surface and wear may not be as high as we might expect, we might see some other thermal effects that could push you into more stops than the computers before might expect you to make.

“I think it was a very solid day and a good feeling. We’ve come out of Monza with a bit of a spring in our step and need to reset and then tick all the boxes on a busy Friday. It was good to see both drivers up there in both sessions.

“We didn’t really see the single lap play out in FP2 because of the crash, and then that curtailed the long runs so again, it leaves us with more unknowns than maybe we’d like as F1 teams going into the race on Sunday. That generally produces the unexpected and something exciting for the fans.”

title: 'A big setback' – McLaren explain Norris' FP2 issue in Madrid
excerpt:
McLaren have confirmed that a gearbox issue prevented Lando Norris from competing in Free Practice 2 ahead of the Spanish Grand Prix this weekend, adding it's "a big setback" for the reigning World Champion.

Drivers and teams got their first taste of the Madring on Friday, with the new venue's part-street, part-purpose-built layout providing a challenge.

Any running was crucial in order to gather data, but Norris' exploits were cut short after just two laps in FP2 before the Briton pulled his McLaren into the garage with a mechanical issue that was not fixed before the end of the session.

"Gearbox problem for Lando, that's obviously a big setback for him," said Mark Temple, McLaren's Technical Director for Performance, after the session. "Going into FP3 we'll be trying to do as much as we can to give him back track time.

"It was as expected, a very technical, tough track for the drivers, trying to find their way and learn the track. Deal with the very hot temperatures on the tyres. For sure track time for Lando will be very important tomorrow."

Norris had been able to finish sixth in the opening hour of practice, nearly nine tenths behind George Russell's Mercedes before his problems later in the day.

Team mate Oscar Piastri was able to complete a full day of running, finishing P8 and P7 across both sessions as the Australian looked to get on top of the new venue.

A particular challenge was finding the right car balance with a compromised set-up for straights and high-speed corners, as well as managing tyre temperature and wear.

"I felt like we got a bit closer in FP2, which was good, but we're still lacking a bit of pace it seems," he said.

"We'll try and improve, it's been an interesting day learning a new circuit. It's certainly tough to get on top of but it's been a day full of learning. Hopefully we can find a bit more tomorrow.

"Trying to extract the performance on a street circuit like this is pretty challenging. That's the biggest thing for us at the moment. Hopefully tomorrow we can make things a bit easier and find just a bit more consistency and a bit more ability to get that time out of the car."

title: Antonelli sets the pace ahead of Leclerc during Madring FP2
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli ended Friday’s running at the Spanish Grand Prix as the fastest driver on track, heading the Ferrari duo of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton in the second hour of practice.

The Italian posted an unbeatable time of 1m 33.662s before the session was halted to recover Arvid Lindblad’s damaged Racing Bulls car, and no one was able to better Antonelli’s lap in the closing minutes, giving him an advantage of just over a tenth.

With a limited amount of time to learn the new circuit, all 22 drivers were eager to make the most of Free Practice and begin to push the limits – ideally whilst avoiding the daunting walls that line the Madring.

Unfortunately for Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin confirmed that he would be forced to miss the beginning of the session due to a clutch issue he suffered following his practice starts in FP1.

Haas’ Esteban Ocon and Ollie Bearman were the first to head out in the high temperatures, leading a long queue of their competitors before George Russell – who topped the times in FP1 – set an early benchmark of 1m 36.011s.

He was soon demoted down the timesheets as Ferrari continued their impressive showing on the medium tyres, with Leclerc claiming the top spot until the standings leader completed his first effort to go over a second clear.

As is expected on a track with a freshly laid surface, the evolution was notable and Leclerc closed the gap to just 0.001s, ensuring that the Mercedes and Ferrari drivers occupied P1-P4 in the opening 15 minutes.

Despite his impressive lap, his team were struggling in the final sector, where they were significantly down on the likes of Antonelli. But they weren’t the only ones facing issues – McLaren opted to change Lando Norris’ gearbox, restricting him to the garage, while Oscar Piastri complained about a lack of rear grip.

Although the Australian managed to improve on the soft compound, his lap was eclipsed by Lindblad, the Racing Bulls driver having consistently impressed through the first sector to wind up just two tenths off Antonelli’s fastest time.

But the lack of incidents couldn’t last forever, and sadly, it was Lindblad who was the first to be caught out. Coming into Turn 13, he lost the rear and crashed into the barriers to bring an early end to his day at the Madring.

Once the subsequent red flag period concluded, Antonelli remained P1 thanks to his earlier rapid time, leaving him ahead of Leclerc and Hamilton on the timesheets. Lindblad similarly held onto P4 from Russell, Max Verstappen and Piastri.

Yuki Tsunoda was eighth for Racing Bulls, followed by Haas’ Ocon and Red Bull’s Liam Lawson. Pierre Gasly claimed P11, the Frenchman leading the Audi pair of Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto, Bearman, Franco Colapinto, and home favourite Carlos Sainz.

Despite his shorter running, Alonso took P17 while Alex Albon, Sergio Perez, Lance Stroll and Valtteri Bottas completed the order, with Norris unable to set a representative time for McLaren.

With the first day of action in Madrid complete, the teams and drivers will have the chance to delve into their learnings overnight before the final hour of practice takes place at 1230 local time on Saturday, September 12.

title: F2: Beganovic flies in Madrid to take second pole of 2026
excerpt:
Dino Beganovic would not be denied top spot in Qualifying around the Madring, earning his second pole position of the 2026 campaign.

The DAMS Lucas Oil and Ferrari Driver Academy talent recorded a 1:44.331 to wind up two-tenths clear of the chasing pack.

Rodin Motorsport’s Alexander Dunne got closest to the Swede, finishing P2 ahead of Championship contender Rafael Camara, who ended the day third for Invicta Racing.

Beganovic and Dunne traded top spot back and forth throughout the Madrid Qualifying session, with the DAMS emerging in the latter stages as the quicker force.

After three red flag stoppages, Beganovic found one last improvement in the final minutes to lower his personal best and provisional pole time. Dunne responded moments later, but couldn’t improve to depose the DAMS driver from P1.

Camara’s session was compromised by the earlier red flags, and he was down in 14th place ahead of his final attempt.

The Brazilian was able to deliver a lap good enough for third under pressure to improve his odds of closing the gap to Championship leader Nikola Tsolov, who finished the session fifth.

Martinius Stenshorne was fourth, while Beganovic’s DAMS teammate Roman Bilinski finished sixth on a strong day for the French squad.

Laurens van Hoepen was seventh, with Noel Leon, Ritomo Miyata and Emerson Fittipaldi completing the top 10.

title: How Sainz became the heart of the Spanish GP in Madrid
excerpt:
As Formula 1 returns to Madrid for the first time in over four decades, with the Madring playing host to the Spanish Grand Prix, it's a particularly special weekend for Carlos Sainz.

The Williams racer's home city is Madrid, and he plays a key role as an ambassador for the event, but it's also a special weekend for the Spaniard's legion of dedicated fans. Quite simply, Sainz means a lot to the city that raised him.

Anyone who has visited Madrid knows it’s a vibrant capital. It brings together the best of Spanish culture, from music to food and art, but for years it was missing the sound and excitement of Formula 1 stopping by for a weekend.

This weekend, that changes, and Carlos Sainz, born and raised in the Spanish capital, grew up dreaming of exactly this: a home race of his own, in the place where he started karting at just 10 years old.

“When I think about Madrid, I think about my first karting races,” Sainz says. “That’s where it all started, where I started dreaming about being an F1 driver.

"Now I get to race in my home town and be the ambassador of the Grand Prix – it’s a privilege, and it’s also a chance to open the door for people from all over the world to discover Madrid at the same time.”

'One of our own'

Sainz calls it an honour to be at the centre of this weekend but, if you ask Madrid-born fans what the Spaniard means to them, and to have him racing in their city, the answers often go way back in time.

“My first real memory of Carlos is his Formula 1 debut, back in 2015 at the Australian Grand Prix", says Bea Quevedo. "He qualified eighth and finished ninth, in the points, on his very first outing, an incredible result for a rookie that nobody expected.

“I remember how thrilling it was to have another Spanish driver on the grid, and not just any driver: someone with that level of raw talent. For those of us in Madrid, it wasn’t just ‘a Spaniard in F1’; it was one of our own, a kid from our city, mixing it with the best in the world.”

Now, after 11 seasons at the pinnacle of motorsport, four victories and 29 podiums, that sense of ownership hasn’t gone anywhere in the decade since – if anything, it’s only deepened now that the sport has finally come to his home.

Madrid's own countdown

Long before lights out, Madrid had already proved it was more than ready for the weekend, living its Grand Prix before a single lap was driven. From the start of the week, fans followed Carlos Sainz's packed schedule, eager to share in the emotion of the occasion, with that passion perhaps best illustrated on Tuesday when Plaza del Callao filled up hours before he even arrived.

For his fan community, Team Fifty5, the pull runs deeper than one race weekend.

“This week, from the moment I landed, the city was already buzzing,” Sainz says. “I went to Callao and there were people there since early morning – different stories, different ages, all gathering together. It was incredible.

"Team Fifty5 has been with me through the good weekends and the bad ones, and seeing that kind of dedication and support in my own city gave me a boost I don’t take for granted.”

For Quevedo, he isn’t just a driver competing here; he’s the reason so much of this excitement feels personal to the people of Madrid. It’s that connection between the city and him that gives this week its soul.

Itziar Blazquez adds that it's that same bond that matters. “Sharing a passion with different people around the world is cool, but sharing the exact same love for the same driver creates a real bond,” she says.

Additionally, being part of the Fifty5 community, “feels like getting a step closer to a big global family that backs him no matter what.”

A home race, literally

For most drivers, a 'home race' usually means having a grandstand and the warmth of a crowd of compatriots, or at least a familiar setting. Monaco, for example, is special for many because they've lived there for years, just a few minutes from the track. For Sainz, Madrid means something far more literal.

“Madrid is my home and I’ve always been very proud of the city and my country,” he says. “I get to spend the weekend with my family and sleep at my parents’ house to then go racing – that doesn’t happen anywhere else on the calendar.

"And then on top of that, I get to do it in front of a Spanish crowd, in the city that watched me grow up. It’s going to be a very special weekend.”

Sainz on bringing F1 back to his home city of Madrid

Carlos Sainz’s legacy in Madrid

Whatever happens on Sunday, fans in Madrid have already made up their minds about what this weekend – and the years leading up to it – mean.

Having lived her whole life in Madrid, Blazquez can vouch for what Sainz represents to the city.

“He's the heart of motorsport in the capital of Spain, he's become a role model,” she says. To her, Sainz is someone who “represents Madrid spirit at its best: his relentless hard work, resilience, and class.”

Her message to him is simple: “You carried Madrid to the top step of the podium, to the world stage, and now you've brought Formula 1 back home. So, thanks.”

title: Mercedes target Madring gains as all upgrades are revealed
excerpt:
A new track like the Madring automatically comes with a wide array of challenges, from finding the perfect racing line to working out how to control tyre degradation. To make it easier – or more complicated, depending on how you look at it – some teams will introduce upgrades over the Spanish Grand Prix weekend. We've rounded up all the details below...

Mercedes

Mercedes have hinted at bringing more significant upgrades later in the season, but for now, they've stuck with circuit-specific changes to generate appropriate load and drag. These include reducing the rear wing central winglet span and adding another winglet behind the exhaust.

The front lip has also been reprofiled to improve flow attachment through all steer conditions, which isn't exclusively for this weekend.

Ferrari

The Scuderia have only got one small update as they've adapted the rear suspension fairing profile, with the aim of returning a local load benefit.

McLaren

Seeking another strong points haul, McLaren have some additional rear wing furniture, improving flow conditioning onto the rear wing mainplane and flap elements.

Red Bull

Building on their work from Monza, Red Bull's main priority for this weekend is reliability. They've altered the rear wheel bodywork assembly to restore the load of earlier races and made a geometric change to the floor bib.

Racing Bulls

Racing Bulls, currently the 'best of the rest' in the Constructors' Championship, haven't submitted any upgrades for the Spanish Grand Prix.

Alpine

After a superb weekend in Italy saw Pierre Gasly claim pole position, Alpine have optimised the forward floor board to improve the local pressure distribution and flow management.

Haas

Haas made numerous adjustments to their chassis and gave Ollie Bearman the latest Ferrari power unit last time out, so haven't brought any further upgrades.

Audi

Audi finished in the points four rounds in a row before their streak came to an end in Italy. They've also decided not to bring any updates to the car this weekend.

Williams

Williams are still holding out for their major upgrade package at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, so Alex Albon and home favourite Carlos Sainz won't have any changes to maximise in Spain. However, they're using Friday's practice sessions to test some components for next year's car.

Aston Martin

It's only been a few rounds since Aston Martin debuted their B-spec challenger in Hungary, so they're taking the time to maximise its performance, as well as that of the updated Honda power unit. To that end, no upgrades have been listed for the Spanish Grand Prix.

Cadillac

Last up are Cadillac, the only team without a point on the board. They've reintroduced an updated central trailing edge winglet on the rear wing flap to generate more rear aerodynamic load and improve stability.

A vane has also been added to the outboard diffuser sidewall, targeting further aerodynamic performance and increased load at the rear of the car.

title: Russell tops FP1 as cars hit Madring for first time
excerpt:
George Russell finished fastest in Free Practice 1 ahead of the Spanish Grand Prix, heading Mercedes team mate Kimi Antonelli as drivers sampled the Madring for the first time.

The Briton posted a 1m 34.077s, which left him nearly three tenths clear of Antonelli, as Ferrari drivers Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton finished best of the rest on Formula 1's return to Madrid.

As the light at the end of the pit lane turned green at 1330 local time, a flurry of cars headed out onto the 22-turn circuit for the first time in a bid to gather as much information as possible across the opening one-hour session.

Sergio Perez was the first driver to encounter a problem, the Cadillac man requiring a new steering wheel, while both Alpines of Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto remained in the garage for the first 15 minutes.

Esteban Ocon reported that "the grip is high", with lap times continually tumbling as drivers utilised the medium Pirelli tyre in the early running and attempted to avoid traffic that was rife around the 5.414km street circuit throughout.

Drivers soon began to exceed the limits, with Antonelli running wide at Turn 13, while both Audi drivers Gabriel Bortoleto and Nico Hulkenberg cut the Turn 5 chicane.

By the halfway point, Hamilton headed the leaderboard with a 1m 34.620s, leaving him fractionally quicker than Leclerc, with Antonelli two tenths further back but having used the soft tyre.

Russell aborted his first lap with the red-walled tyre after encountering traffic, with Liam Lawson using the same compound to jump up to fourth inside the final 30 minutes with his Red Bull.

Russell was soon back up to speed, slotting into third behind the Ferrari drivers and ahead of Antonelli as the track continued to evolve and tyre management started to become an issue, Max Verstappen having grained his medium tyres.

There were problems for Yuki Tsunoda as his Racing Bulls machine was wheeled into the garage with 20 minutes remaining, the Japanese driver suffering an issue with his power steering that ended his session.

By this stage most drivers were focused on single lap pace, Russell posting a 1m 34.145s before fractionally improving down to a 1m 34.077s which remained fastest at the chequered flag.

In contrast, Leclerc was struggling to improve with the soft tyre, heading into the run-off zone at Turn 17, as Antonelli jumped up to second and less than three tenths behind Russell approaching the final 10 minutes.

Leclerc finished nearly five tenths behind Russell, as Hamilton on the medium tyre, Verstappen's Red Bull, Lando Norris (McLaren), Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls), Oscar Piastri's McLaren, Hulkenberg and Lawson completed the top 10.

Bortoleto was P11 from Ocon's Haas, Colapinto, Gasly, home hero Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin) and Ollie Bearman's Haas.

Spanish local Carlos Sainz was P17 in his Williams, followed by Tsunoda, Lance Stroll's Aston Martin, Alex Albon (Williams) and the two Cadillacs of Perez and Valtteri Bottas.

title: McLaren name 'absolute' Lando Norris priority after 'significant' setback
excerpt:
McLaren has named ensuring Lando Norris gets the maximum possible track time in FP3 at the Spanish Grand Prix as its "absolute priority."

Norris missed all of FP2 at the Madring - aside from two slow laps - with a gearbox issue, reporting that the process of losing it, the 'box had gone into 'false neutral.'

It means the world champion has lost one-third of the total practice time available at the new Spanish GP venue, and will be on the backfoot heading into FP3, where he must condense his qualifying simulations and race pace runs into the sole hour remaining.

Reflecting on the tough day, McLaren's engineering technical director, performance, Mark Temple explained that the team's priority was to ensure Norris maximised that sole remaining hour as it also worked through a "deep dive" to put the MCL40 into a competitive performance window.

"Today presented a significant challenge, particularly with the gearbox issue that cost Lando a substantial amount of track time in FP2," Temple explained.

"It's a big setback on a new and technically demanding circuit like this, where every lap is crucial for gathering data. The conditions are tough for everyone, with high temperatures and low grip, so losing that running time certainly puts us on the back foot heading into Saturday.

"Our focus tonight is on a deep dive into the data to see where we can unlock more performance. The car isn't quite where we want it to be, but we have some clear ideas on both the chassis and driver side to explore.

"We'll be working hard to analyse a wider variety of potential changes than usual to ensure we can give both drivers a more competitive package for qualifying. Maximising Lando's track time in FP3 will be our absolute priority to help him recover."

title: Fernando Alonso reveals 'near impossible' task at new Spanish GP circuit
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has explained he faces a task he has described as "nearly impossible" in his attempt to salvage a crumb of home comfort this weekend.

On the opening day of the Spanish Grand Prix weekend at the new Madring circuit in Madrid, Alonso's FP2, in particular, was badly compromised by a clutch issue with his Aston Martin at the start of second practice he suffered following his practice starts at the end of FP1.

As Alonso noted, the lack of early running in that session put him "out of sync", and "a little bit behind the programme", completing just 16 laps in contrast to a number of drivers who posted lap totals in the mid-20s.

Alonso eventually finished 17th quickest, offering a glimmer of hope he may qualify in Q2, albeit aided by the fact that McLaren's Lando Norris failed to post a time due to his MCL60 encountering a gearbox problem which required a change.

Assessing what might be possible going into the race, the two-time F1 champion does not doubt that the imposing 22 corners of the Madring will mean "it's going to be hard to overtake".

As for himself in the AMR26, he said: "For us, nearly impossible with the deficit on the straight, so qualifying will be important.

"At the same time, with the walls that close, the possibilities of a safety car or red flags, all these kinds of things, we need to stay focused. We need to see the chequered flag, do our own race.

"Whatever is the result in qualifying, I think there's still hope for Sunday, if we do a perfect execution of the race."

[Article continues below]

Alonso calls for 'fix' on 'a couple of things

Surprisingly, despite the pre-event suggestion there would be numerous incidents in the lead-up to the weekend given the tricky nature of the track, there was only one red flag across the two hours of practice running.

That was sparked by Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad 35 minutes into FP2 as he lost control of the rear of his car through the fast Turn 13 left-hander.

Traffic was also a problem, as Alonso discovered, and whilst he is confident of an improvement in qualifying, there are ongoing issues with the Honda power unit that will not aid his cause.

"It was tricky out there with the traffic, but it was our mistake to be out of sync," said Alonso. "Tomorrow in quali should be better.

"But it's going to be tricky to get it right, with tyre temperature and battery state of charge at the end of the lap, sometimes, if you do a different driving style in the last few corners, it seems that we are very sensitive to that with the Honda power unit.

"There are a couple of things that we are discovering, and we need to fix for sure."

title: Alex Albon airs major concern over new Spanish GP icon
excerpt:
Alex Albon has shared the concerns he holds about Turn 12 at F1's new Spanish Grand Prix venue, the Madring.

La Monumental, as it has been dubbed, is a 550m-long banked corner in the middle of the lap, and features around 24 degrees of banking.

It was created to be the standout corner of the circuit, which has taken over Spanish Grand Prix hosting duties from Barcelona, and will be the 79th different circuit to host a world championship grand prix.

However, after preparations for the weekend, including a track walk, Albon has aired two big concerns he holds about the corner, related to safety during and after the on-track running, especially in the race.

"There are a lot of high-speed corners, a lot of blind corners; it gives me vibes of Macau, but more for an F1 track. It is a little bit concerning: the blind spots in some of the corners," Albon told media, including RacingNews365.

"Like if there is a car that's stopped on the other side of the corner, I hope they're just quick on the VSCs and the red flags. Inevitably, there are going to be a few crashes this weekend.

"Turn 12 itself is high-speed. I am quite concerned about the cool-down laps when drivers are doing slow laps. I don't think there's a correct place you can position the car. If you put the car up top, actually, I think the line is a little bit to drift up to the middle of the track, and then you come back again, so you're not in a perfect place.

"I worry about the marbles in the race. It's very low grip. At this point in the weekend, they resurfaced the track quite late. I think it was May, which, if you think about what the last resurfaced track we did when the oils are still coming off the track, Turkey [in 2020] is like the most recent standout one that we've had. You then form a single line because all the rubber is only in one place, and if you stray away from that line, then there's no grip.

"So on top of trying to find clean air and going up high on the banking, you've also got you'll you'll have marbles to contend with as well later into the race, so you've got to be careful with that.

"I personally don't think you can do that many lines. The track's quite narrow, and it's different when you have clean air, and there's space. Whereas, if you have a little snap, you're into the wall immediately. Drivers aren't as willing to stick it up to the top of the banking and take the risk of running a high line. I hope I'm proven wrong, but I don't think that part of the track is going to offer that much overtaking."

The article continues below.

Alex Albon concerns over Turn 12 - La Monumental

Owing to the length of La Monumental, it is a corner that does not have a defined apex as such, with drivers continually turning through to navigate.

This is something Albon believes is against a driver's natural muscle memory to find the apex.

"I like to go on a scooter, and I like to drive the track eye level or walk the track eye level. Just literally sit on my scooter and go around," he said.

"You really get a different immersion of how little visibility there is around some of the corners, so, if you think about these long, long corners, there's no apex point, and a lot of the corners, actually, if you look at the way the track is, they're late apexes.

"So you're kind of swinging in from a blind spot, and you've got to kind of try and pick an imaginary spot that's a few hundred metres in front of you; that's really challenging to do as a driver.

"It is a lot of repetition and muscle memory just to get that timing right because you basically can't see an apex, so now you're just using your internal body clock and almost imagining.

"You're trying to focus on a reference point to something to know what your apex point of that corner, so that's going to be difficult.

"When you're low down [in the cockpit], obviously the visibility is a lot harder, so that will be interesting."

title: Kimi Antonelli strikes back in FP2 as Madring claims its first victim
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli responded to Mercedes team-mate George Russell topping FP1 at the Spanish Grand Prix, by going quickest in FP2 at the Madring, which saw the first red flag of the F1 portion of the weekend.

Kimi Antonelli topped FP2 at the Spanish Grand Prix, beating Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton in the second and final free practice session of the day.

Arvid Lindblad continued to impress at the Madring, going fourth fastest, just ahead of George Russell in the second Mercedes.

However, the Racing Bulls driver would bring out a red flag with just over 20 minutes of the session remaining, heavily damaging his car and ending his afternoon.

Fernando Alonso had a late start to the session, with the clutch problem he experienced at the FP1 carrying over into the start of FP2, although he would eventually get out on track, going P17.

At the foot of the timing boards was Lando Norris, who had a gearbox failure. McLaren replaced it in the back of his MCL40, but it cost the British driver the rest of his session.

Check out the full FP2 reports at the Spanish Grand Prix below!

Kimi Antonelli strikes back in FP2 as Madring claims its first victim

# Driver Team Time Tyre

Results are being loaded...

Opening salvo

Before the session had even got underway, Alonso faced the prospect of a late start after the clutch issues he suffered following his practice start in FP1 persisted.

The majority of the field quickly filed out onto the circuit, with just Lance Stroll — in the other Aston Martin — and Alex Albon holding back. However, within five minutes, they would both join their peers on track.

Like in FP1, Ferrari set the early benchmark, with Leclerc putting in a 1:35.557, some 45 milliseconds quicker than Hamilton in the second SF-26.

With seven minutes gone, Antonelli would put the hammer down in a meaningful way, going over a second quicker and into the sub-1:34.5s.

At McLaren, Norris returned to the garage with a gearbox issue. It had gone into false neutral, necessitating further investigation as the reigning F1 drivers' champion disembarked his MCL40. The team would eventually confirm a complete change was required, and he would not return to the track.

As the fight between Mercedes and Ferrari at the sharp end intensified, Antonelli found himself frustrated by the Cadillac of Sergio Perez, taking to team radio to say that it is "always" the six-time grand prix winner in the way.

Verstappen thrust himself into the battle just before the 20-minute mark, going quickest. However, his lap time was promptly deleted for track limits, dropping the Dutchman back down to eighth.

Middle third

Alonso would eventually venture out onto the circuit to get his session underway, with the clutch issues on his AMR26 seemingly solved.

25 minutes into the hour, there was a brief yellow flag because of marshals walking down the fast lane of the pit lane, bizarrely.

Arvid Lindblad continued his impressive afternoon, going third fastest in his Racing Bulls. Despite being bumped down to fourth by Hamilton in short order, the pace of his VCARB 03 caught attention in the paddock.

The Ferrari driver, not for the first time at the Madring, subsequently held up Yuki Tsunoda the following lap, for which he apologised to the 26-year-old.

A few minutes later, Lindblad lost the rear of his car at the entrance to Turn 13, slamming sideways into the barriers on the outside of the corner, bringing out a first red flag — in F1 — of the weekend.

The Briton's usual team-mate, Liam Lawson, also had a moment, although significantly less severe. The Isack Hadjar stand-in glanced the wall on the outside of Turn 21 before the session was interrupted.

Closing stages

The session resumed with just under 15 minutes remaining, but it was not a case of 'as you were' for Verstappen at Red Bull. The four-time F1 drivers' champion immediately came on the radio to claim that his steering felt strangely heavier than before.

Lawson remained in the garage, unable to return to the circuit, but there would be little movement on the timing board over the final quarter of an hour, with the field prioritising longer runs.

In the dying moments, Stroll was told to go slowly with his Aston Martin nursing a suspected — but undisclosed over team radio — issue. As such, Antonelli stayed atop the standings uncontested at the end.

title: FIA president makes Fernando Alonso vow over F1 retirement fear
excerpt:
FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has stated he will do all he can to convince Fernando Alonso to continue in F1 next season.

Alonso has not yet confirmed if he will remain part of the F1 grid in 2027, as he mulls over his options.

The two-time champion has endured a challenging F1 campaign with Aston Martin, who has slipped towards the rear of the pecking order at the start of the sport's new era under fresh technical regulations.

He detailed in the build-up to the Madrid race weekend that he also has an option to race for Aston Martin in the World Endurance Championship next year.

But Ben Sulayem insisted he has spoken to Alonso in a bid to sway him to stick around for 2027.

“There is no way we can allow Fernando, a great champion, to leave just because of the circumstances,” Ben Sulayem said at the New Economy Forum in Madrid.

“That's not the way to leave the stage. He has to be successful and then he leaves whenever he wants - not because of the performance.

“I share the issues, the car is not performing. I met with Lawrence [Stroll] yesterday, and I am going to do the changes.

“I will talk to him [Alonso] to try and make him change his mind. It's not acceptable.

“I heard some rumours, when I saw him, he didn't mention it. When I see him, I will be speaking to him.

“I said to him, 'I saw him [Alonso] very sad'. I said, 'Fernando, it's not acceptable that you are coming to your country after now, a two-time world champion, and you are last'.”

Ben Sulayem points to ADUO change behind Honda boost hope

While Aston Martin has struggled for form, so too has its engine partner Honda.

The Japanese manufacturer has an aid in the ADUO system, which allows those who are behind the benchmark to allocate extra resources to their engine in a bid to improve.

The FIA made further changes to it earlier this year - allowing those who are vastly adrift to have even more of a chance to catch up.

Ben Sulayem suggested it was a direct measure to help Honda.

“We did something earlier in May, legally, for the team, towards the engine, to go and improve,” he said.

“Then I said to him, 'I'm not going to tell you what we are going to do. Please tell me what you want, you are the driver - come and tell me what you want us to do to improve this result'.

“Suddenly, you see everything change.”

title: Red Bull eyeing Baku return for Isack Hadjar
excerpt:
Will Isack Hadjar be ready for the next grand prix in Azerbaijan?

Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies is hopeful Isack Hadjar could return for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix later this month as he continues to recover from a wrist injury.

For the third successive race weekend, Hadjar is sidelined after fracturing a wrist sustained whilst boxing training shortly before the Dutch Grand Prix at the end of August.

Hadjar also missed last weekend's Italian Grand Prix, and has again been reduced to a watching brief for this weekend's Spanish Grand Prix at F1's newest circuit, the Madring situated in Madrid.

Mekies said the decision to keep Hadjar out of the Spanish GP was straightforward.

"It was an easy one," he said, speaking to Sky Sports F1. "He didn't feel that he was 100%, and that's the only criteria we use. Are you 100%? So it was an easy one for here.

"We have always said we will prioritise him coming back at 100%. There was no point in throwing him into a track like here, not feeling good and potentially delaying his full recovery. So that's the assessment we made."

Baku comeback on the cards for Hadjar

The Azerbaijan Grand Prix on September 26 gives Hadjar an additional two-week window to complete his recovery.

Striking a positive tone on the 21-year-old's progress, Mekies said: "We have a bit more time before Baku.

"Honestly, there is nothing wrong with his recovery. The recovery is going as planned. Some things take time, and we will take the time to evaluate before Baku and to put him on the sim."

The Baku City Circuit, a demanding street track, would represent a challenging environment for Hadjar's return, though simulator work in the coming days should offer Red Bull a clearer picture of his readiness.
